name: torsion-latch
title: Torsion Latch
description: A destructive-action switch wound like a torsion spring: dragging the knob winds a visible SVG coil against rising resistance, release before the over-center point and it springs back, push past it and the stored energy whips the switch on.
useWhen: a destructive toggle (kill switch, maintenance mode, delete protection) where the confirmation cost should be continuously felt as stored physical tension during the drag itself, not gated by a timer — pick hold-to-confirm for a single press-and-hold destructive action with no travel/position of its own, or frostbite-switch for an ordinary styled binary flip with no bistability or confirmation cost at all.
instruction: A destructive-action switch (real <button role=switch aria-checked>, 136x56 track) whose knob both translates and rotates: dragging couples translateX linearly to a 0-270deg rotation, so the knob visibly spins as it slides. An Archimedean spiral (a single precomputed SVG path, no per-frame recompute) sits behind the knob and winds with it — revealed progressively via stroke-dashoffset against an explicit pathLength=1000 (0 at rest, fully drawn at full travel), its whole coil group scaling down ~6% as tension rises, and its stroke color interpolated live from --border toward --foreground (parsed from getComputedStyle at mount, re-derived on a MutationObserver watching documentElement class changes, so both themes stay legible). Dragging is not 1:1: a falling-gain curve (a Gaussian dip centered on an over-center fraction at 58% of the travel) makes the same pointer-pixel delta buy less knob travel as the knob nears that point and more on either side of it, so the resistance is actually felt building toward the peak. On release the physics alone decide the outcome, with no separate code branch for intent: released with progress below the over-center point, an underdamped spring (k=70, zeta=0.22) carries the knob home with 2-3 diminishing overshoots, exactly like released spring tension; released past it, a stiff spring (k=200, zeta=0.9, matching this registry's established snap-detent feel) whips it to the far stop with one small overshoot settle, and the switch commits at that instant (aria-checked flips before the visual finishes catching up — the decision is physical, the settle is cosmetic). A pointercancel mid-drag (losing the pointer) aborts back to whatever was last committed, never counting as intent. Keyboard cannot drag, so Space/Enter (native <button> click) substitutes a compressed 350ms eased wind. Because an instant keypress has none of a drag's built-in safety margin, the destructive direction (off to on) is two-phase: the first press winds only to the over-center point and holds there, armed — announced through a visually-hidden aria-live=assertive status region — and a second press within 3 seconds completes the whip to on; left alone for 3 seconds it un-winds itself on the same underdamped spring and announces the cancellation. The safe direction (on to off) is single-phase, matching what a real drag release below the over-center point already does. A pointerdown always cancels any pending arm/spring and takes over from the live position. prefers-reduced-motion keeps the exact same two-press safety gate (motion preference is not a reason to remove a destructive-action confirmation) but collapses every transition — wind, whip, spring-back — to an instant jump to its end frame, spiral included. disabled dims the control and ignores all input. Controlled/uncontrolled via checked/defaultChecked/onCheckedChange, mirroring this registry's other switches; an external controlled change animates to the new state directly, bypassing the arm gate (that gate exists for user-initiated activation, not a parent re-render). Zero dependencies; tears down its MutationObserver, media-query listener, rAF and arm timer on unmount.
